title: Evidence for Chapter 29: the Great Depression abroad and the gold standard, 1929-1936
source: Hansard of 21 September 1931 (House of Commons and House of Lords) and the Gold Standard (Amendment) Act 1931; Keynes, 'The End of the Gold Standard' (27 September 1931, Essays in Persuasion); Hoover's statement of the moratorium (the American Presidency Project); the Federal Reserve Bulletin (July, August, September and October 1931, December 1935, October 1936); the Silver Purchase Act of 1934 (48 Stat. 1178); Foreign Relations of the United States 1934 and 1935 (the silver question); Bernanke and James (1991, NBER chapter c11482); Bernanke (NBER Working Paper 4814, 1994); Eichengreen and Sachs (NBER Working Paper 1498, 1984); Brandt and Sargent (1989); the abstract of Friedman (1992) on IDEAS/RePEc; Díaz Alejandro (1983, NBER chapter c11185); the Banco Central de la República Argentina; Wolf (CEP Discussion Paper 834, 2007); the authority records of the Library of Congress and the BnF
series: Evidence rows: id, place, year, values (';' separated, in the order of the quotation), unit, source key, page or document, the source text verbatim (empty for a value read on a page image), note
license: Quotations for criticism, scholarship and teaching, each with its source; no full original is redistributed. Hansard: 'Contains Parliamentary information licensed under the Open Parliament Licence v3.0.' The Gold Standard (Amendment) Act 1931 (legislation.gov.uk): 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.' Keynes died in 1946; his essays are in the public domain in the United Kingdom (the copy used is named in source keynes1931). Works of the United States government are in the public domain: the presidential statement (the American Presidency Project asks for the credit 'Online by Gerhard Peters and John T. Woolley, The American Presidency Project'), the Federal Reserve Bulletin, the Statutes at Large and Foreign Relations of the United States. NBER Working Paper 4814: '© 1994 by Ben S. Bernanke. All rights reserved. Short sections of text, not to exceed two paragraphs, may be quoted without explicit permission provided that full credit, including © notice, is given to the source.' (row b95_copyright). NBER Working Paper 1498 and the NBER chapters c11482 and c11185 print no copyright line; they are quoted in short phrases with their source. Brandt and Sargent (1989): '©1989, Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. (North-Holland)' (row bs_copyright); short phrases only. Friedman (1992): the abstract's notice 'Copyright 1992 by University of Chicago Press.' (row fr92_copyright); short phrases only. The BCRA's site: 'Copyright © 2006-2025 | Central Bank of Argentina | All rights reserved'; short phrases only. Wolf (2007): '© N. Wolf, submitted 2007', all rights reserved; short phrases only. The authority records of the Library of Congress (id.loc.gov) are public data; those of the Bibliothèque nationale de France (data.bnf.fr) are metadata reused under the Licence Ouverte (Open License); Wikisource (keyneslife) is CC BY-SA. The chapter's Chinese renders the quotations; translations are the book's own.
notes: Every quotation is checked word for word against the cached source text by data/fetch/verify_web_quotes.py, and every value is read from its quotation by checks/check_ch29.py; rows with an empty quotation are values read on a page image (sources nberc11482img, nberw1498img, nberc11185img), named as such in their notes. The OCR of the Federal Reserve Bulletin interleaves the columns of a page, so its sentences are quoted in the parts that are contiguous, with the whole sentence in the note. OCR misprints are kept in the quotations and named in the notes (Hansard 'Amendmont'; the Act 'Septeml)er'; Keynes ',^200,000,000', '2 5', 'Anierica', 'eflFort'; the Bulletin '4}£'; Eichengreen and Sachs 'IPl935', 'preceeded' and their misprint '141 percent' for 41; Bernanke (1995) 'Ml' for M1). Indirect testimony: Eichengreen (1992) through Bernanke (1995) and Wolf (2007); Friedman and Schwartz (1963) and the Chinese Emergency Decree of 3 November 1935 (from the Chinese Yearbook 1936-37) through Brandt and Sargent (1989); Silber (1977) through Díaz Alejandro (1983); Tamagna (1942) through Brandt and Sargent. Not obtained: Eichengreen (1992, Golden Fetters), the Journal of Economic History version of Eichengreen and Sachs (1985), the text of Friedman (1992) beyond its abstract, the Chinese text of the decree of November 1935 (zh.wikisource answered 429), and the Macmillan and May reports of 1931. The table snapshots of the chapter are depressionworld_goldexits, depressionworld_es, depressionworld_silver, depressionworld_yuan_monthly and depressionworld_china.
citation: See the 'source' field; each row names its source key in the 'sources' object.
